chapter: Harlem, Redman's band and the Savoy
title: Chick Webb trading arrangements and humming solos
summary: Hinton recalls Webb on Broadway singing whole arrangements and trading charts; Jackson recalls him humming Taft Jordan's solo at the Savoy.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Great drummers: who they admired and why

blocks.x: That's my whole recollection of Chick Webb just standing on the corner of 48th and Broadway. He was like a trader. He liked to trade arrangements, you know. He was always concerned only -- His only concern was for that band.

And I can remember my last recollections of Chick, he's standing on that corner and he's telling me, "Milt, I got a new arrangement,, and the saxophones go like this, do de-de-de-do do-do, in the reeds, and the trombones go, dit dee dee." Then I say, "r-r-r-p." He was singing --
--in a good conversational list and you couldn't get away from him. You know, you'd be a little bored sometime with him when he got into his second or third arrangement.

He's telling you, "And Bobby's going to play this here," and then he'd go, de-de do do-do-do. And he'd be standing down there waiting for Chu Berry because Chu Berry had promised, told him that he was going to give him two Cab Calloway arrangements for one of his Bennie Carter arrangements. He would trade arrangements.
He was beautiful. He was so beautiful, Chick was, and he was such a lovable guy.
Everybody that did knew him loved him, you know.

And Don and I used to go up to the Savoy all the time to hear him and that's how I knew about him knowing about solos because he'd come out and tell Don, he said, "Did you hear what Taft played that last chorus?" and hum Taft's whole solo. Taft Jordan.
